questions.title: A strength the outside world is quietly converting into a threat
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.1 SWOT analysis and 6.3 STEEPLE analysis (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
questions.challenge_mechanism: Management's SWOT lists the eighteen-year leaflet contract as its leading strength and recommends defending it, but STEEPLE shows the decline in printed leaflets is driven by social and technological change outside the firm, so the same contract is a threat the internal analysis cannot see and the admitted weakness in packaging design is where the opportunity actually lies.

stimulus.title: Calderbank Print & Packaging
stimulus.body:
Calderbank Print & Packaging is a family printing firm in a market town, employing 40 people. For eighteen years it has printed the weekly leaflets of a supermarket chain under a rolling annual contract that is renewed each spring. Each year the directors write a SWOT: they have again listed the supermarket contract as the business's greatest strength and 'no experience of packaging design' as a weakness, and they propose to spend EUR 60,000 on a faster leaflet press to protect the contract.

Around the firm, however, the market is moving. Shoppers increasingly use supermarket apps instead of paper leaflets, and a rival has installed a digital press that prints short runs cheaply. The government has introduced a tax on virgin paper and placed extended producer responsibility for packaging waste on producers. Energy costs for the presses have risen by about 40% in two years, and trade customers now ask for recyclable cardboard cartons rather than plastic film. Local environmental groups have publicly praised firms that cut paper use.

The table shows how the firm's revenue has actually moved across its three service lines over the last three years.

table.caption: Calderbank revenue by service line, years ended 31 March (EUR 000).

questions.question: The directors of Calderbank Print & Packaging must decide whether to spend EUR 60,000 on a faster leaflet press or to invest in packaging capability instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a SWOT analysis and a STEEPLE analysis differ in what they can tell the directors, using one example of each from the case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the table, calculate each service line's share of total revenue in 2023 and in 2025, the change in total revenue over the period, and revenue per employee in each year. Comment on what the figures show.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether Calderbank should follow the SWOT and spend EUR 60,000 on the leaflet press, or act on the STEEPLE findings instead. Justify your answer.

questions.answer:
(a) SWOT is an audit of the firm's own position. It sorts factors into strengths and weaknesses, which are internal and controllable, and opportunities and threats, which are external, and it is used to match the firm's resources to its environment. STEEPLE examines the external environment alone, across social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical factors, and is used to identify change that the firm does not control. (A1)(A1)

The difference matters here. The case example for SWOT is the supermarket leaflet contract, which the directors call a strength because it is long-standing and gives a predictable order book. The case example for STEEPLE is the social and technological shift away from printed leaflets towards supermarket apps, which is outside the firm's control and is shrinking the market for the product it prints. (A1)(A1)

(b) Total revenue: 2023 = 900 + 250 + 150 = EUR 1,300k; 2025 = 590 + 610 + 170 = EUR 1,370k. (M1)(A1)

Shares of total: leaflet printing falls from 900/1,300 = 69.2% to 590/1,370 = 43.1%; packaging rises from 250/1,300 = 19.2% to 610/1,370 = 44.5%; signage rises from 150/1,300 = 11.5% to 170/1,370 = 12.4%. (A1)

Total revenue rose by EUR 70k, or 5.4%, so the business looks as though it is growing. Revenue per employee: 2023 = 1,300,000/40 = EUR 32,500; 2025 = 1,370,000/40 = EUR 34,250. (M1)(A1)

The comment mark is for seeing that the headline is misleading. The total is up only because packaging has grown by 144%, from EUR 250k to EUR 610k, while the line the directors are defending has fallen by EUR 310k, or 34.4%, and is now smaller than packaging. The firm's future is already being decided by the line its SWOT calls a weakness. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The SWOT points one way. The leaflet contract is the firm's oldest relationship and its largest single order, and losing it would remove about 43% of revenue at a stroke. Spending EUR 60,000 on a faster press lowers the unit cost of the work the contract needs and may make Calderbank the cheapest bidder when the contract is next renewed. On this reading the EUR 60,000 protects the core of the business.

The STEEPLE reading contradicts it. The fall in leaflet revenue is not caused by anything inside the firm: readers are moving to apps, the supermarket has begun cutting print volumes, and the tax on virgin paper and extended producer responsibility raise the cost of the very product the press would print. A faster press makes Calderbank better at producing something its customer is buying less of. The weakness the SWOT admits, no packaging design experience, sits in the one line that is growing, and packaging faces rising demand because of the same environmental and legal pressures that are hurting leaflets. (A1)(A1)

A defensible answer can still support the press, because it buys time and cash while packaging capability is built. But the strongest answers notice that the two tools classify the same contract differently, as a strength internally and a threat externally, and recommend using the leaflet cash flow to fund packaging rather than to defend the declining line. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) One mark for each of the two tool descriptions and one for each correctly applied example. A candidate who describes SWOT and STEEPLE accurately but uses no case example earns at most two. Do not credit a SWOT that lists only internal factors or a STEEPLE that includes the firm's own capabilities.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the two totals and (A1) for the shares; accept shares to one decimal place. Award (M1)(A1) for revenue per employee. The comment mark requires the candidate to contrast the falling leaflet line with the rising packaging line; a candidate who reports only that total revenue grew forfeits it. Follow through on arithmetic slips.

(c) The two discriminating marks are for recognising that the decline is externally driven and that the admitted weakness sits in the growing line. A candidate who simply repeats the SWOT and recommends the press cannot earn more than two marks, however well written. Credit a conclusion that keeps the press only if it is justified by timing or cash flow, not by the claim that leaflets will recover. Do not credit generic statements about the internet that are not tied to the case.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the two tools disagree about the same fact. The directors' SWOT is not careless: the supermarket contract really is the firm's largest and oldest relationship, and losing it would remove roughly 43% of revenue. Read internally, it is a strength and defending it is rational. Read through STEEPLE, the same contract is a threat, because the force reducing it - the shift to apps, the paper tax and extended producer responsibility - lies entirely outside the firm and cannot be managed by a better press.

The lever is that the obvious tool is the wrong one. A student who reaches for SWOT because the case is about the firm's position will produce a tidy four-box list and recommend the investment, but the analysis cannot show the trend, because a SWOT is a snapshot of factors, not a model of change. STEEPLE reveals the direction of travel, and the revenue table makes it quantitative: leaflets fall from 69.2% to 43.1% of revenue while packaging rises from 19.2% to 44.5%, so the firm's centre of gravity has already moved.

The trap is the total. Revenue rises by EUR 70k, or 5.4%, and revenue per employee rises from EUR 32,500 to EUR 34,250. A candidate who checks only these concludes that the business is healthy and the contract worth defending. The figure that contradicts this is the 34.4% fall in the leaflet line and the fact that it is now smaller than the packaging line the SWOT calls a weakness.

Classic wrong turns: treating the packaging weakness as a reason to stay with leaflets; listing STEEPLE factors without linking them to the falling line; and recommending diversification without noticing that the capability to diversify already exists inside the firm.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Toolkit nodes 6.1 (SWOT analysis) and 6.3 (STEEPLE analysis). The scenario was constructed so that the factor management records as its leading internal strength is reclassified as a threat once the external environment is scanned, and so that a rising total revenue of EUR 1,370k conceals a 34.4% fall in the firm's largest line. The company, the environmental drivers, the revenue table and every figure are original and were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Totals 900 + 250 + 150 = 1300 and 590 + 610 + 170 = 1370. Shares: 69.2%, 43.1%, 19.2%, 44.5%, 11.5%, 12.4%. Total change 70k = 5.4%. Revenue per employee 1,300,000/40 = 32,500 and 1,370,000/40 = 34,250. Leaflet fall 310k = 34.4%; packaging rise 360k = 144%. Swept against the HL-only list: no 2.5 culture, 2.7 industrial relations, 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets, 4.3 forecasting, 4.6 international marketing or any 5.3/5.6-5.9 content, and no HL-only Toolkit tool (no Gantt, critical path, force field, Hofstede, Porter, contribution analysis or linear regression); the Toolkit tools used are SWOT and STEEPLE only.

questions.title: Two matrices, one product, opposite instructions
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.2 Ansoff matrix and 6.4 Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
questions.subtopic: 6.2 Ansoff matrix and 6.4 Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix
questions.challenge_mechanism: The BCG matrix tells Brackenwood to harvest its cash cow and starve its dog, but the Ansoff matrix shows that the only low-risk growth open to the firm is market development of exactly that cash-cow product, and that the product BCG calls a star can only be grown by diversification the firm cannot fund, so the two tools give opposite instructions for the same product.

stimulus.title: Brackenwood Pet Foods
stimulus.body:
Brackenwood Pet Foods is a family-owned manufacturer of dry dog food, based in one factory and selling through pet shops and a small number of garden centres. The directors use the BCG matrix each year to decide where to invest, measuring market share within the premium dog-food segment, and they use the Ansoff matrix whenever they consider a new product or a new market.

The premium segment is worth EUR 150 million a year. Supermarket own-label dog food, which Brackenwood does not supply, is a separate value segment three times larger. Against the whole dog-food market, Brackenwood's best-selling product, Adult Complete, has a share of 11%, while the value-segment leader has 13%.

The directors treat market growth of 10% or more a year as high, and a relative market share of 1.0 or more as high. The table gives the four main products.

columns: Largest rival's share of premium segment (%)
table.caption: Brackenwood's four main products, premium dog-food segment, year to 31 March 2026.

questions.question: The directors of Brackenwood Pet Foods must decide where to invest over the next three years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, calculate the relative market share of each of the four products and classify each one using the BCG matrix. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the Ansoff matrix would classify two growth options open to Brackenwood, using examples from the case.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether Brackenwood should follow the BCG recommendation to harvest Adult Complete. Justify your answer with reference to the Ansoff matrix and to the market data.

questions.answer:
(a) Relative market share = own share divided by the largest rival's share. Puppy Complete 22/20 = 1.10; Adult Complete 34/18 = 1.89; Senior Care 7/26 = 0.27; Grain-Free Fresh 9/24 = 0.38. (M1)(A1)(A1)

Growth: Puppy Complete 14% (high), Adult Complete 3% (low), Senior Care 2% (low), Grain-Free Fresh 16% (high).

Classification: Puppy Complete is a star, with high growth and high relative share. Adult Complete is a cash cow, with low growth and high relative share. Senior Care is a dog, with low growth and low relative share. Grain-Free Fresh is a question mark, with high growth and low relative share. (A1)(A1)

(b) Ansoff classifies growth by whether the product and the market are existing or new. Market development means an existing product sold into a new market: Adult Complete sold through the supermarket value channel, which Brackenwood does not currently supply. The product already exists; only the market is new. (A1)(A1)

Market penetration means more of an existing product sold into the existing market: winning more shelf space for Adult Complete in the pet shops and garden centres it already uses. (A1)

Also creditable: product development, such as new Grain-Free recipes for existing premium customers, and diversification, a new product for a new market, which is the riskiest quadrant. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The BCG reading is clear. Adult Complete has a relative market share of 1.89 and market growth of only 3%, so it is a classic cash cow: the matrix says take its cash and invest it in the star, Puppy Complete. On the premium-segment numbers this is textbook, and harvesting means withdrawing promotion and product development from Adult Complete rather than reinvesting in it.

Ansoff contradicts that instruction. The lowest-risk growth available to Brackenwood is market development: taking the existing Adult Complete product into the supermarket value segment. That is a new market for an existing product, the second-least-risky quadrant, and it needs investment, which is exactly what harvesting removes. So the BCG instruction to take cash out of Adult Complete would close the one low-risk growth option the firm has.

The data make the clash worse. The classification depends on how the market is defined. Measured against the premium segment, Adult Complete has a relative share of 1.89; measured against the whole dog-food market, its share is 11% against the value leader's 13%, a relative share of 0.85, which is a dog, not a cash cow. The same product carries opposite BCG labels. The tool cannot settle the question until the directors decide which market they intend to compete in, and that is a strategic choice, not a calculation.

A defensible answer can still harvest: the firm is small, Puppy Complete is the star, and cash is scarce. The strongest answers notice that harvesting Adult Complete would destroy the Ansoff option the same product makes possible, and recommend funding market development of the cash cow instead. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the relative-share method and (A1)(A1) for the four correct figures. Award (A1)(A1) for the four correct classifications; a candidate who misclassifies one product but applies the 10% and 1.0 rules consistently earns one of the two. Accept 0.38 or 0.375 for Grain-Free Fresh and 0.27 for Senior Care. A candidate who computes relative share as the largest rival divided by the firm's own share reverses the matrix and cannot earn the classification marks.

(b) Two marks for market development correctly identified and applied to the supermarket channel; one mark for a correctly applied market penetration example; one further mark for either product development or diversification correctly applied. Do not credit new product, new market as market development.

(c) The discriminating marks are for seeing that the Ansoff market-development option requires the very investment that BCG harvesting removes, and for noticing that the cash-cow label depends on the premium-segment definition. A candidate who simply repeats the BCG classification and recommends harvesting cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that harvests only if it is justified by the firm's lack of funds, not by the claim that Adult Complete has no growth left.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that two accepted tools give opposite instructions about the same product. On the premium-segment data, Adult Complete is a textbook cash cow: 3% growth and a relative share of 1.89, five times the 0.38 of the question mark. The BCG logic is to take the cash it generates and put it into the star, Puppy Complete. A student who does the classification correctly and stops there will recommend harvesting.

Ansoff changes the answer, because it asks a different question. BCG asks where the cash is; Ansoff asks how risky growth would be. The least risky growth Brackenwood has is market development, the existing Adult Complete product sold into the supermarket value segment, which is precisely the product BCG has told the firm to stop investing in. Harvesting the cash cow and pursuing the Ansoff option are mutually exclusive, and the case does not say which the directors should prefer.

The lever is that the BCG classification is not a fact but a consequence of a choice about the market. Premium segment: relative share 1.89, cash cow. Whole market: 11% against 13%, relative share 0.85, dog. The matrix is often taught as though market share were given; here it is defined by the directors, and changing the definition changes the instruction. That is the point the strongest answers reach, and it is what makes the question a decision rather than an exercise in plotting.

Classic wrong turns: treating the BCG label as objective; recommending investment in the star without noticing that the firm has no cash because the cash cow is being harvested; placing market development in the diversification quadrant, which overstates its risk; and forgetting that the same product can be a cash cow and a dog at the same time.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Toolkit nodes 6.2 (Ansoff matrix) and 6.4 (BCG matrix). The scenario was constructed so that the two tools prescribe opposite actions for one product: BCG harvests the cash cow while Ansoff identifies the same product's market development as the firm's least risky growth, and so that Adult Complete's relative market share is 1.89 in the premium segment but 0.85 against the whole market, flipping its BCG classification. The company, portfolio, segment sizes and every figure are original and were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Relative market shares: 22/20 = 1.10, 34/18 = 1.89, 7/26 = 0.27, 9/24 = 0.38. Total portfolio revenue 24 + 46 + 9 + 15 = 94; Adult Complete is 46/94 = 48.9% of it. Whole-market relative share 11/13 = 0.85. Growth rules checked: 14 and 16 are high, 3 and 2 are low. Swept against the HL-only list: no 2.5 culture, 2.7 industrial relations, 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets, 4.3 forecasting, 4.6 international marketing or any 5.3/5.6-5.9 content, and no HL-only Toolkit tool (no Gantt, critical path, force field, Hofstede, Porter, contribution analysis or linear regression); the Toolkit tools used are the Ansoff and BCG matrices only.

questions.title: A mean that says grow and a spread that says do not
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics (the SL Toolkit). P2 Section B.
questions.challenge_mechanism: Management's decision tree uses a 0.6 probability of high demand that the twelve monthly observations contradict, because the mean of 77 customers a day conceals a bimodal split between a cluster near 42 and a cluster near 125, so the empirical probability of 5/12 reverses which option has the higher expected value once the loan interest is deducted.

stimulus.title: Foxglove Bakery
stimulus.body:
Foxglove Bakery runs a single shop in a market town and is considering a second outlet. Two sites are available on the same high street: a small kiosk, which would cost EUR 40,000 to fit out, and a large cafe, which would cost EUR 120,000. Both would be financed by a bank loan at 6% a year, and the directors compare annual profit after interest.

The directors have two sets of profit forecasts, before interest, for each option. If demand is high, the kiosk would make EUR 40,000 a year and the cafe EUR 120,000. If demand is low, the kiosk would still make EUR 10,000, but the cafe would lose EUR 60,000 a year.

The finance director has assumed a 0.6 probability of high demand, based on her reading of the local economy. The marketing director disagrees. She has collected the daily customer numbers from a trial stall that traded in the same high street, with the same opening hours, for twelve months. Her figures are in the table, and she defines a high-demand month as one in which the stall served more than 80 customers a day.

table.caption: Daily customers at the trial stall, months 1 to 12.

questions.question: The directors of Foxglove Bakery must decide whether to open a kiosk or a cafe as the second outlet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table, calculate the mean, the median and the range of daily customers, and comment on how well the mean represents a typical month.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the probability of a high-demand month from the trial data. Then calculate the expected annual profit after interest of each option using the finance director's probability and using your estimate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate which option Foxglove Bakery should choose. Justify your answer with reference to your decision tree and to the descriptive statistics.

questions.answer:
(a) The twelve monthly figures are 40, 45, 38, 42, 120, 130, 125, 44, 41, 118, 135 and 46, giving a total of 924 customers a day across the months. (M1)

Mean = 924/12 = 77 customers a day. (A1)

Ordered, the two middle values are 45 and 46, so the median = (45 + 46)/2 = 45.5 customers a day. (A1)

Range = 135 - 38 = 97 customers a day. (A1)

The mean is a poor summary of a typical month. It is 31.5 customers a day above the median, and no month was close to it: five months clustered near 42 and five near 125, with the remaining two between. The distribution is bimodal, not symmetrical, so the mean describes a month that never happened. (A1)

(b) High-demand months are those above 80 customers a day: months 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11, so five of twelve. The trial estimate of the probability of high demand is 5/12 = 0.417. (M1)(A1)

Using the finance director's 0.6: kiosk = 0.6 x 40,000 + 0.4 x 10,000 = EUR 28,000; cafe = 0.6 x 120,000 + 0.4 x (-60,000) = EUR 48,000. (M1)(A1)

Interest: kiosk loan 40,000 x 6% = EUR 2,400; cafe loan 120,000 x 6% = EUR 7,200. Net expected profit: kiosk EUR 25,600; cafe EUR 40,800. (A1)

Using the trial estimate of 5/12: kiosk = (5/12) x 40,000 + (7/12) x 10,000 = EUR 22,500; cafe = (5/12) x 120,000 + (7/12) x (-60,000) = EUR 15,000. After interest: kiosk EUR 20,100; cafe EUR 7,800. (A1)

The two probabilities therefore rank the options differently.

(c) Indicative evaluation. On the finance director's probability the decision is straightforward. The cafe's expected profit of EUR 40,800 is more than half as much again as the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and the upside, EUR 120,000 in a good year, is the kind of return that would justify the larger loan. A decision tree drawn on a 0.6 chance of high demand points clearly to the cafe.

The descriptive statistics undermine the probability the tree uses. The mean of 77 customers a day is not a typical month: it sits between two clusters, and the median of 45.5 is the better guide to what most months look like. Five of the twelve months were high-demand, so the empirical probability is 0.417, not 0.6. Rerun with 5/12, the ranking reverses: the kiosk earns EUR 20,100 against the cafe's EUR 7,800. The kiosk is also the more robust choice, because its worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000 while the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the whole investment.

The evaluation therefore turns on the probability, and the probability is the one thing the directors cannot observe. If the town's economy really does deliver high demand six years in ten, the cafe is right; if the trial stall is representative, the cafe destroys value in most years and the interest payment makes the bad case worse. The strongest answers note that a decision tree is only as good as its probabilities, that the trial was one stall in one year, and that opening the kiosk first keeps the option open. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1)(A1) for the mean, (A1) for the median and (A1) for the range. The comment mark requires the candidate to notice that the mean is well above the median and that the data are bimodal; a candidate who says only that the mean is 77 forfeits it. Accept 45.5 for the median.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for identifying the five high-demand months and the probability of 5/12; accept 0.42 or 41.7%. Award (M1)(A1) for the two expected profits on the 0.6 probability and (A1) for the interest and net profits; then (A1) for the two expected profits on 5/12 and their net values. Follow through on arithmetic slips, but a candidate who omits the interest in one option and not the other cannot reach the evaluation marks.

(c) The discriminating marks are for rerunning the expected values with the empirical probability and for noticing that the ranking reverses. A candidate who reports the mean of 77 and recommends the cafe cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that chooses the cafe only if it is justified by evidence about the local economy rather than by the finance director's assumption. Do not credit answers about the cafe's menu or staffing.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the decision tree gives a clean answer on an input the case contradicts. With a 0.6 probability of high demand the cafe's expected profit, EUR 40,800 after interest, is well above the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and a student who draws the tree and computes the expected values will recommend the cafe. The arithmetic is not the trap; the probability is.

The lever is that descriptive statistics can invalidate the input to a decision tree. The twelve monthly observations are bimodal: five months near 42 customers a day and five near 125, with nothing in between. The mean of 77 therefore describes no real month, and the median of 45.5 is the honest summary. Counting the months above the 80-customer threshold gives a probability of 5/12 = 0.417, not 0.6. Substituting it reverses the ranking, and the loan interest widens the gap: the cafe falls to EUR 7,800 while the kiosk holds at EUR 20,100.

The second lever is the shape of the downside. The kiosk's worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000; the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the investment. A mean and an expected value treat these symmetrically, but a small bakery facing a EUR 60,000 loss does not. The range of 97 customers a day is the number that carries this: it says demand is not merely uncertain but bimodal, and bimodal demand is exactly where a single expected value is least trustworthy.

Classic wrong turns: using the mean of 77 as though it were typical; treating the 0.6 probability as data rather than an assumption; forgetting the interest; and comparing the cafe's upside with the kiosk's expected value instead of comparing like with like.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Toolkit nodes 6.6 (decision trees) and 6.7 (descriptive statistics). The scenario was constructed so that the twelve monthly observations are bimodal, making the mean of 77 unrepresentative and the empirical high-demand probability 5/12 rather than the assumed 0.6, so that recalculating the decision tree's expected values reverses the ranking of the two options once the loan interest is deducted. The company, the trial data, the probabilities and every figure are original and were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Customer data sum 924, mean 77, median 45.5, range 97; five months above 80 so 5/12 = 0.4167. Expected profits before interest: kiosk 0.6 x 40000 + 0.4 x 10000 = 28000 and (5/12) x 40000 + (7/12) x 10000 = 22500; cafe 0.6 x 120000 + 0.4 x (-60000) = 48000 and (5/12) x 120000 + (7/12) x (-60000) = 15000. Interest 40000 x 0.06 = 2400 and 120000 x 0.06 = 7200. Net: kiosk 25600 and 20100; cafe 40800 and 7800, so the ranking reverses. Swept against the HL-only list: no 2.5 culture, 2.7 industrial relations, 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets, 4.3 forecasting, 4.6 international marketing or any 5.3/5.6-5.9 content, and no HL-only Toolkit tool (no linear regression, which is HL, is used; the statistics are mean, median and range); the Toolkit tools used are decision trees and descriptive statistics only.

questions.title: A circular plan that pays back only at a reuse rate the trial never reached
questions.subject: Business Management SL
questions.syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.5 Business plan and 6.8 Circular business models (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
questions.subtopic: 6.5 Business plan and 6.8 Circular business models
questions.challenge_mechanism: The business plan's payback of 3.8 years rests on an assumed twenty uses per glass bottle, but the three-month trial achieved only six and the break-even is seven, so the circular model the plan presents as a cost saving is dearer per delivery than the plastic it replaces, while the bank's four-year payback rule and the founders' zero-waste objective pull in opposite directions.

stimulus.title: Dale & Vale Dairy
stimulus.body:
Dale & Vale Dairy delivers milk and cream to 3,000 households on five rounds. Each household receives five bottles a week, fifty-two weeks a year. The milk is currently sold in single-use plastic bottles that cost EUR 0.12 each; the bottles are not collected.

The founders, Ravi and Meg, want to switch to returnable glass bottles as part of a circular business model and have written a business plan to raise the money. The plan assumes that each glass bottle will be used twenty times before it is broken or lost. Glass bottles cost EUR 0.60 each, and a bottle washer, crates and a chilled store would cost EUR 180,000. Collecting, washing and handling a returned bottle would cost EUR 0.03 each time it is used. The plan presents the switch as a cost saving and shows a payback period the bank will accept.

The bank lends to the dairy only if the investment pays back within four years.

Before committing, Ravi and Meg ran a three-month trial with 200 households. In the trial each glass bottle was used, on average, six times before it was broken or lost. The founders believe the rate would improve once customers were used to the system, because the trial households were told about the scheme only a week before it began. Ravi argues that the plan's figures are the right ones because they describe how the scheme will work once it is established, and that the dairy has a public commitment to remove single-use plastic. Meg is not sure the dairy can afford to be wrong.

questions.question: The founders of Dale & Vale Dairy must decide whether to commit to the returnable glass scheme in the business plan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a circular business model such as returnable glass bottles could reduce Dale & Vale's costs, and one way in which it could increase them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the figures, calculate the cost per delivery and the total annual cost of bottles and washing under plastic, under the plan's assumption of twenty uses, and under the trial's six uses. State the break-even number of uses and the payback period the plan implies.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the business plan's proposal to switch to returnable glass bottles is sound. Justify your answer with reference to the trial, the bank's lending rule and the founders' objectives.

questions.answer:
(a) A circular business model keeps materials in use rather than disposing of them after one cycle. Two ways it could cut Dale & Vale's costs. First, a glass bottle that is reused replaces many single-use bottles, so the dairy stops buying a new EUR 0.12 plastic bottle for every delivery. Second, it avoids the waste-disposal and packaging charges attached to single-use plastic and reduces exposure to future levies on single-use packaging. (A1)(A1)

One way it increases costs: the model needs reverse logistics. Bottles must be collected from households, returned to the depot, washed and refilled, which adds handling cost and requires the EUR 180,000 washer and store. The dairy also bears the cost of bottles that are broken or never returned. (A1)(A1)

(b) Annual deliveries = 3,000 households x 5 bottles x 52 weeks = 780,000 deliveries. (M1)(A1)

Plastic: cost per delivery EUR 0.12; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.12 = EUR 93,600. (A1)

Plan (20 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/20 + 0.03 = EUR 0.03 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.06; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.06 = EUR 46,800. (M1)(A1)

Trial (6 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/6 + 0.03 = EUR 0.10 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.13; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.13 = EUR 101,400. (A1)

Break-even uses: 0.60/u + 0.03 = 0.12 gives u = 0.60/0.09 = 6.67, so a glass bottle must be used at least seven times to be cheaper than plastic. (A1)

Payback on the plan's figures: annual saving = 93,600 - 46,800 = EUR 46,800; payback = 180,000/46,800 = 3.8 years. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The plan is internally consistent and looks attractive on its own assumptions. At twenty uses a bottle, glass costs EUR 0.06 a delivery against EUR 0.12 for plastic, a saving of EUR 46,800 a year, and the EUR 180,000 is repaid in 3.8 years, inside the bank's four-year rule. The bank's condition is therefore satisfied on the plan's numbers, and the circular model also delivers the founders' environmental objective.

The trial contradicts the assumption on which the whole plan rests. At six uses, glass costs EUR 0.13 a delivery, more than the plastic it replaces, and the annual cost rises to EUR 101,400, about EUR 7,800 a year worse than doing nothing. The break-even is seven uses, so the trial is not close: it falls below the point at which the investment stops destroying value. On the trial evidence the payback never arrives, and the bank's four-year rule is not met.

The evaluation therefore turns on a judgement about the trial. Ravi's argument has some force, because the trial lasted only three months and customers were told about the scheme a week before it began, so six uses may understate a mature scheme. Meg's argument is that the dairy cannot afford to be wrong, and the shortfall is a recurring EUR 7,800 a year, not a one-off. The strongest answers note that the plan should be rewritten with a range of reuse rates, that the scheme should be re-trialled with proper notice, and that the founders' zero-waste objective could be pursued at a smaller scale before EUR 180,000 is committed. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) One mark for each of the two cost reductions and one for the cost increase, each correctly explained; naming reuse without explaining the saving earns at most one. Credit avoided bottle purchases, disposal charges and future levies. Do not credit the claim that it is good for the environment as a cost reduction.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the 780,000 deliveries, (A1) for the plastic cost, (M1)(A1) for the plan's cost per delivery and annual cost, (A1) for the trial cost, (A1) for the break-even of seven uses and (A1) for the 3.8-year payback. Follow through on arithmetic slips. A candidate who uses 0.60/20 without adding the EUR 0.03 washing cost cannot reach the evaluation marks, because the omission is the error the question tests.

(c) The discriminating marks are for the trial cost of EUR 0.13 and the recognition that six uses is below the break-even of seven. A candidate who accepts the plan's twenty uses and concludes that the switch is clearly worthwhile cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that proceeds with the scheme only if it is justified by the trial's weakness or by a staged rollout, not by the claim that customers will return bottles out of goodwill.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the business plan is arithmetically perfect and rests on a single assumption the case has already tested. On twenty uses a bottle, glass costs EUR 0.06 a delivery, saves EUR 46,800 a year and pays back the EUR 180,000 in 3.8 years, just inside the bank's four-year rule. Every figure the plan contains is correct. The mistake is not in the arithmetic but in the reuse rate, which the plan treats as a design choice and the trial reveals as an empirical result.

The lever is that the circular model inverts its own cost logic at a break-even the plan never states. Reuse replaces the repeated purchase of EUR 0.12 plastic bottles, but it adds reverse logistics: collection, washing and handling at EUR 0.03 a delivery, plus the capital cost of the washer. Break-even is 0.60/0.09 = 6.67 uses, so a bottle must survive seven trips before glass is cheaper. The trial managed six. Below that line, the more circular the model, the more it costs per delivery.

The clash of criteria is the second layer. The bank will lend only against a four-year payback, which the plan meets and the trial does not; the founders have a public zero-waste commitment, which the plan advances and the trial postpones. Neither objective can be satisfied at once on the evidence given, so the answer is a decision about which risk to accept, not a calculation. That is why the strongest answers propose rewriting the plan with a range of reuse rates and re-trialling with proper notice, rather than simply rejecting the scheme.

Classic wrong turns: accepting the plan's twenty uses; computing cost per delivery without the EUR 0.03 washing cost; treating the break-even as one use rather than seven; and concluding that the circular model must be cheaper because it is more sustainable.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL Toolkit nodes 6.5 (business plan) and 6.8 (circular business models). The scenario was constructed so that the plan's payback of 3.8 years depends on an assumed twenty uses per glass bottle while the trial achieved six and the break-even is seven, so the circular model is dearer per delivery than the plastic it replaces, and so that the bank's payback rule conflicts with the founders' zero-waste objective. The company, the trial, the cost structure and every figure are original and were recomputed numerically.

verification.method: Every figure recomputed in Python. Deliveries 3000 x 5 x 52 = 780000. Plastic 780000 x 0.12 = 93600. Plan cost per delivery 0.60/20 + 0.03 = 0.06, annual 46800, saving 46800, payback 180000/46800 = 3.846 years. Trial cost per delivery 0.60/6 + 0.03 = 0.13, annual 101400, which is 7800 more than plastic. Break-even uses 0.60/(0.12 - 0.03) = 6.67, so seven uses are needed. Swept against the HL-only list: no 2.5 culture, 2.7 industrial relations, 3.6 efficiency ratios, 3.9 budgets, 4.3 forecasting, 4.6 international marketing or any 5.3/5.6-5.9 content, and no HL-only Toolkit tool (no Gantt, critical path, force field, Hofstede, Porter, contribution analysis or linear regression); the Toolkit tools used are the business plan and circular business models only.
